From Construction Accident Reports

ABSTRACT The time-intensive extraction of insights from textual safety documents using conventional
methods causes delays and inaccuracies, hindering proactive incident prevention in construction projects.
While the architecture of large language models (LLMs) were well-studied, their deployment efficiencies
were often overlooked. This study proposes DistilBERT as a more efficient text management method for
extracting safety text from construction safety documents. To maintain the relevance of the extracted safety
text, a dataset of 5,224 construction accident cases from 73 projects across the Euro-Asia region was
compiled, where incidents were analyzed through detailed questionnaires to identify safety attributes, with
term frequency-inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) analysis applied for validation. When benchmarked
against conventional NLP methods and state-of-the-art LLMs such as BERT, RoBERTa, and XLNet,
DistilBERT demonstrated comparable accuracy with significantly reduced computational time. Specifically,
DistilBERT achieved an accuracy of 79% in severity scale classification with an F1 score of 0.72,
while reducing processing time by approximately 50% compared to BERT (from 2,918.28 seconds to
1,492.08 seconds). By offering rapid inference speeds with negligible accuracy trade-offs, DistilBERT
emerges as a practical tool for automating safety text extraction, making it ideal for settings with limited
computational capabilities and urgent decision-making requirements. This study examines how DistilBERT
can be integrated into construction safety management systems without modifying the underlying platforms.
Future work should focus on API creation, secure machine learning pipelines, and optimized deployment of
LLMs, particularly in complex contexts.

Given this rich reserve of information, numerous stud-
ies have gravitated towards employing machine learning
(ML) [2], [3] and particularly, natural language processing
(NLP) methods due to their adeptness at parsing complex
datasets [4], [5]. The manual evaluation of safety reports is
intricate and demands significant resources, as each safety

to understand human language by processing and analyz-
ing text structure and word meanings [6], [7], providing
mechanisms to retrieve information, organize, and interpret
the data [1], [4]. Specifically, despite existing literature
on digital technologies integration for safety management

safety performance of specific activities rather than the entire
construction process, such as the management of safety
text [8]. Yet, organizations still need to enhance their ability
to manage safety by implementing more structured and
forward-thinking strategies that involve greater participation
and are seamlessly incorporated into business operations [9].

Recent advancements in computational hardware and
the scaling law of model capabilities have facilitated the
development of sophisticated large language models (LLMs)
[11] capable of harnessing the wealth of construction safety
data. This growth is in line with the scaling law, which
suggests that increasing the scale of models and training
data consistently enhances model capability, facilitating the
development of sophisticated LLMs [11].
Recent research has established the potential of pre-
trained ML models in transforming NLP methods into
the new era of LLMs [12], retrieving information from
extensive datasets [13]. Beyond their higher prediction
accuracy, LLMs possess a remarkable ability to understand
text sequences [14], enabling them to interpret chronological
order and causality in incident reports, which is crucial for
identifying underlying risk factors. Unlike traditional NLP,
which treats text as a bag of words, LLMs maintain the
sequential integrity of language, preserving the narrative
flow that is essential for understanding complex construction
scenarios. However, the increased computational resources
required for larger models pose challenges in terms of
efficiency and practicality for real-world applications.
Although the architectural and training principles of
LLMs had been widely documented, the field had largely
overlooked systematic evaluation of model efficiency and
data adaptability in real-world deployments, particularly in
construction-based applications. This study demonstrated
that resource-heavy models, such bidirectional encoder
representations from transformers (BERT) [15] architectures,
where the higher computational time can cause memory or
computational bottlenecks through deployment phase.
Correspondingly, DistilBERT [16] a distilled version of
BERT [15] proposed that offers a more efficient alternative
with reduced size and faster inference times while retaining
much of the performance. This trade-off between speed,
model size, and accuracy is particularly important in
construction safety management scenarios, where real-time
processing and limited computational resources can constrain
the applicability of larger LLMs, often requires the use of
high-performance graphics processing units (GPUs) [11].
By demonstrating that DistilBERT can achieve comparable
accuracy with significantly reduced computational resources
and faster inference times, we aim to provide a more efficient
text management method for extracting safety text from
construction safety documents. A dataset comprising 5,224
construction accident cases across 73 projects in the Euro-
Asia region was collected and used to evaluate the proposed
method. To ensure LLMs focus on context rather than word
repetition, we used TF-IDF to quantify the significance of
words in the ‘‘Explanation’’ narratives of accident reports.
TF-IDF measures document content and specifically word
importance based on their frequency in a document relative
to the entire corpus, without assigning semantic meaning or
context to the words [17], [18].

selection section then compares the proposed method’s per-
formance with other LLMs and conventional NLP methods.
Finally, the framework for integrating LLMs into safety
management offers a practical implementation approach,
including a dashboard demonstration and procedural steps.

B. RESEARCH BACKGROUND ON LLMS
LLMs as subcategory of NLP, are artificial intelligent systems
that are trained on large amount of dataset [39]. They surpass
conventional NLP systems in terms of performance and
adaptability [40]. Compared to methods such as manual
categorization and analytical higher process (AHP) used
previously, LLMs offer advantages regarding efficiency,
accuracy, and adaptability. With their pre-trained weights,
LLMs can leverage downstream NLP tasks [41] to provide
text generation and language-related tasks with high accu-
racy [42].
The advances of LLMs in the AI field [42] resulted in
their widespread application in both research and commercial
settings [43], positioning LLMs as instrumental tools in
both academic research and commercial applications [44].
A wide range of tasks can be performed by tailoring general-
purpose LLMs to specific fields through the integration of
domain-centric data, incorporation of specialized knowledge,
and a focus on domain objectives [11]. For instance, [39]
developed LLMs to classify constraints in construction
planning meetings, uncover discussion patterns, and extract
root causes for constraints. LLMs such as BERT [15] and
generative pre-trained transformer 4 (GPT-4) [45] are NLP
methods that have been trained with deep learning approaches
to generate useful textual responses [46], [47].
The launch of BERT by Google in 2018 is widely
regarded as a pivotal moment in NLP’s evolution [48], with
recent years witnessing its diverse applications such as stock
price prediction [49], categorizing urgent posts [50], essay
valuation [51], and different sentiment analysis tasks [7], [52]
in different languages [53]. Particularly, in the construction
sector, [15] have applied multiple BERT models to pre-
dict construction litigation judgments, calculating similarity
between cases and predicting court judgments with high
accuracy. The capabilities of BERT extend from language
translation to enhanced communication. Thus, it has been
applied by [54] at the pre-design phase of construction to
process quality objectives and needs in the Italian public
tender context. The most notable use of BERT, however, has
been in the development of question-answering systems and
Chatbots. Reference [55] used BERT and natural language
generation to develop a conversational query answering
system for building information modeling (BIM) and thus
help construction personnel access building information.
In another study, [56] adopted BERT for a question-and-
answer Chatbot, which is an efficient way of accessing
research-based information in architecture, engineering, and
construction domains. Parallel to these developments, BERT
has also been adapted to create construction specifications
through the extraction of identified information from exten-
sive construction documents [57].

C. PROBLEM STATEMENT AND RESEARCH OBJECTIVES
A vast amount of data exists within this construction
management domain, predominantly in natural language text
form, encapsulating decades of safety reports, incident logs,
and compliance documentation. LLM applications in the
construction sector are still limited [61]. Despite limited
research on LLM on management of construction safety text,
BERT has shown promise in the construction safety field
for tasks such as text mining [56], detecting risk clauses
in contracts [59], and hazard identification at construction
sites. While BERT is adept at extracting features from safety
texts, its bidirectional nature might not fully capture the
sequential dependencies in incident narratives as effectively
as more advanced LLMs. An LLM like BERT comes with
challenges such as high computational time [7] and their
opaque nature [62], limit their practicality in real-world
applications in construction safety management.
D. RESEARCH GAPS AND CONTRIBUTIONS OF THE
CURRENT STUDY
Research demonstrating the application of BERT in a specific
phase of construction also opens up the prospect for a broader
exploration of advanced LLMs in the context of construction
safety management. Particularly, while the recent application
of LLMs in different fields underscore the effectiveness of
BERT but also raises questions about the potential of more
advanced language models in this domain. Building on the
BERT architecture and to improve the efficiency of extraction
procedure of safety text, this study proposes DistilBERT [16],
a more efficient LLM that distills the knowledge of BERT
from the same datasets but with a focus on retaining most of
its performance while significantly reducing the model’s size
and complexity.
DistilBERT potential is due to their transfer learning
ability, which uses pre-trained weights on a large text cor-
pus [11] and is thus built on a rich foundation of pre-learned
linguistic patterns and contexts. It can potentially attain
superior accuracies, a position reinforced by the integration
of domain-specific data and steadfast alignment with industry
objectives [11], thus aligning with the imperative to enhance
predictive safety models [21], [63], [64], [65] and providing
a robust, data-driven foundation for safety decision-making.
This pre-learned knowledge is a byproduct of training on
extensive datasets, often encompassing diverse topics and

label columns. The severity column requires the model to
extract four distinct classes from the 5,524 records, which is
relatively close to the function of an ML classifier. However,
the activity column presents a more complex challenge, with
nine distinct classes needing to be extracted from each of the
5,524 records. This requires the model to accurately identify
and differentiate between a wide range of activities associated
with construction accidents. While the occupation column
does not present as many classes, it still contains five different
categories, each posing its own set of predictive challenges.

X. CONCLUSION
This study has demonstrated that DistilBERT serves as
a more efficient text management method for extracting
safety text from construction safety documents. By focusing
on DistilBERT, we addressed the limitations of conven-
tional NLP methods and larger, resource-intensive LLMs,
providing a practical solution that balances performance
and efficiency. Four state-of-the-art LLMs pre-trained on
domain-specific datasets and processed for training have been
tested and compared, namely BERT, RoBERTa, XLNet, and
DistilBERT.
Through the analysis of 5,224 construction accident cases
across 73 projects in the Euro-Asia region, DistilBERT
achieved comparable accuracy to larger models like BERT
while significantly reducing computational time. For exam-
ple, in severity scale classification, DistilBERT attained
an accuracy of 79% with an F1 score of 0.72, reducing
processing time by approximately 50% compared to BERT
(from 2,918.28 seconds to 1,492.08 seconds). In addition,
we have paid careful attention to the evaluation of DistilBERT
and by integrating TF-IDF analysis and cosine similarity
validated the significance of the extracted information. This
enhances trust in the model’s output and facilitates better
decision-making.
Overall, the proposed approach addresses two underex-
plored gaps: (1) a focus on data evaluation (via TF-IDF and
similarity checks) to avoid model bias and data leakage, and
(2) explicit consideration of a model’s efficiency and crash
resilience in real-world scenarios. We highlight that large
LLMs may falter on large or complex texts, emphasizing
how DistilBERT remains reliable when integrated into
typical construction project workflows that depend on stable,
continuous data processing.
The integration of DistilBERT into construction safety
management allows replacing time-intensive expert judgment
with an efficient, automated solution. By focusing on an
efficient LLM, this study contributes to practical applica-
tions where computational resources and time are critical
considerations. DistilBERT’s ability to extract relevant
safety attributes efficiently enhances predictive capabilities
and decision-making processes in the construction sector,
aligning safety imperatives with efficiency and project
objectives. When integrated into platforms like Procore (for
project management and safety) and Aconex (for document
control and collaboration), DistilBERT brings automated
classification of incident reports, real-time tagging, and a
human-in-the-loop feedback system. This can support native
ML model uploads, externally connected, offering sophis-
ticated NLP capabilities without modifying the platforms
themselves. Future research must focus on enhancing the
integration of LLMs in construction management through
advancements in API development, plugin creation, and
secure external ML pipelines. Such improvements would
enable continuous data updates, model training, and seamless
LLM integration, directly enhancing safety and decision-
making. Furthermore, it is essential to highlight that
practical deployment of LLMs in complex construction
sites is likely to encounter significant challenges. Future
research should focus on testing these models, assessing
their efficiency, cost, and performance, both with expert
involvement and directly in real-world sites. Research should
explore efficient LLM deployment, particularly emphasizing
lightweight models like DistilBERT, which provide reliable,
data-driven outcomes and reduce response variability. Given
the significant financial requirements of models like GPT-
4 o1, future studies should explore the complementary
use of efficient, cost-effective LLMs, ensuring that high-
performance capabilities are accessible without excessive
resource expenditure.
